item.passage:
Pharaoh would not stay on the scale. Every time Maya set him down on the steel plate, the desert tortoise stretched out his scaly front legs, found the edge, and tipped himself off onto the counter with a sound like a dropped dinner plate. The red numbers jumped to two kilos and something, then back to zero.

Maya had volunteered at the Larkspur Animal Clinic every Saturday since September. Mostly she folded towels and refilled the water bowls in the waiting room, but today Dr. Benedetti had handed her the clipboard for Mr. Pyle's tortoise and said, "Monthly weigh-in. He knows the routine."

If Pharaoh knew the routine, he had decided against it. Mr. Pyle, who was eighty-one and had owned the tortoise since before Maya's mother was born, sat in the plastic chair by the door with his cane across his knees. "In the old days I'd just hold him and stand on the bathroom scale," he said. "Then my knees retired before I did."

Maya tried a leaf of romaine, held just beyond the edge of the plate. Pharaoh lunged for it and walked off the scale to get it. She tried covering his eyes with a folded towel, which Luis, the veterinary technician, had once told her calmed some animals. Pharaoh pushed the towel off with his head and kept going.

She stood back and looked at the scale. It was the same kind they had at the deli counter of the supermarket where her father shopped, a flat plate with a row of buttons under the numbers. She thought about the deli clerk, who always set an empty plastic tub on the plate and pressed a button before spooning in the potato salad, so that the tub itself weighed nothing on the ticket.

In the supply closet she found a gray plastic dishpan with sides about six inches high. She set it on the plate. The numbers read 412 grams. She pressed the button marked TARE, and they went back to zero.

Then she lifted Pharaoh, who swam his legs in the air in protest, and set him in the pan. He walked to one side and pushed his head against the plastic. He walked to the other side and did the same. The numbers wavered and settled: 2,318 grams.

Mr. Pyle leaned forward on his cane. Maya checked the clipboard. Last month's weight, in Dr. Benedetti's handwriting, was 2,309.

"Nine grams," she said. "He gained nine grams."

"That's about a strawberry," Mr. Pyle said. He sat back, and for the first time since he had come in, he set the cane against the wall.

When Dr. Benedetti came in a few minutes later, she found the dishpan still on the scale and a strip of masking tape across its side, on which Maya had written in marker: TORTOISE. DO NOT REMOVE. TARE FIRST.

item.passage:
The lifeguard blows the long whistle at five
and nobody moves. We hang on the gutter
in a row like laundry, chins on the warm lip,
pretending the sound was meant for someone else.

All summer the pool has been the shape of our days:
the rope of floats that kept the deep end deep,
the clock on the snack bar with its cracked face,
the smell of chlorine we carried home in our hair.

Tomorrow they will drain it, or whatever
it is they do, and the water we have argued in,
raced in, floated in face-up like starfish,
will slide off somewhere under the parking lot.

The second whistle. Marisol goes first,
up the ladder slow, as if each rung were a year.
Then the twins, then me. The concrete burns
our feet, and we walk on our heels to the fence.

From the bleachers the water looks
like something that has already forgotten us,
blue and flat, a few leaves turning on it,
the lane lines rocking for no one.

Someone's little brother is still in the shallow end
and his mother calls his name three times,
and each time he answers "one more minute,"
and each time she gives it to him.

I would like to tell him what I know,
that minutes run out whether you ask or stay quiet,
but I am thirteen and dripping and I want
the same thing he wants, and I say nothing.

item.passage:
The summer I was sixteen I worked at the Hollister Farm corn maze, ten acres of field corn cut into paths in the shape of a giant rooster that only made sense from the air. My job was to sit on a wooden platform in the middle, a kind of lifeguard chair eight feet up, and help people who were lost.

On the first day Mrs. Hollister gave me a map of the maze, a red flag on a pole, and one piece of advice. "Do not tell them the way out," she said. "Tell them where they are." I thought this was a strange distinction, and a little unkind, since most of the people who waved at me from the paths had been walking for an hour and wanted only to leave.

I learned what she meant in my second week. A father with two small children called up to me from a dead end near the rooster's tail, and because the children were crying I simply gave him directions: left, left, right, straight past the scarecrow, right again. Ten minutes later he was back at the same dead end, more frustrated than before. Somewhere between the second left and the scarecrow he had made a wrong turn, and once he had, every instruction after it led him somewhere new.

The next time, I tried it Mrs. Hollister's way. I waved my flag and told a lost family that they were in the rooster's comb, the jagged part at the top of the head, and that the exit was below the beak. I could see them stop and study the map printed on their tickets. Then the mother pointed, the family turned around, and I watched them work their way down the neck on their own.

Directions, I realized, only worked if you never made a mistake. A location worked even after you had made several. A family that knew it was in the comb could fix its own wrong turns, because it could always ask again where it was and compare the answer with the map. A family following my list of turns could only start over.

By August I had stopped giving directions at all. People would shout, "Which way?" and I would shout back, "You're in the left wing!" and some of them shook their heads at me, at first.

I think about the platform more often than I would have guessed. Last year my younger brother called me from a highway rest stop, lost, his phone's battery almost gone, and asked me how to get to my apartment. I started to give him the turns. Then I stopped and asked him what he could see.

item.prompt: According to the author, why does the single line at the post office feel slower than it really is?
choices: The recorded voice calls out the window numbers too slowly.
People in it are unable to see which clerk is working fastest.
It is folded so that customers seem to walk away from the front.
Its clerks spend longer with each customer than cashiers do.
Its whole length is in plain view of the people waiting in it.
item.passage:
Every supermarket I have ever shopped in offers the same small test of character at the checkout. There are six lanes, each with its own line, and you must pick one. You look at the carts. You count the items in them. You note the man with the coupons and the woman who is still on the phone, and you choose the lane that seems shortest. Then you watch the lane beside you move faster, as it always seems to, and you begin to calculate whether it is worth switching.

I have switched. Everyone has. I have abandoned a perfectly good place behind a single carton of milk for the lane next door, only to arrive just as its cashier switched on the little light that means a price check. I have watched the person who had been behind me in my old lane reach the register first, and I have pretended to read a magazine about celebrities whose names I did not know.

The post office near my apartment does things differently. There is one line, folded back on itself between two rows of posts and ropes, and it feeds four clerks. When a clerk is free, a recorded voice calls out a window number, and the person at the front goes. Calculating and switching are both beside the point. You simply wait your turn.

The single line feels slower, because it is long and you can see all of it. In fact a single line feeding several clerks is, on average, at least as quick as separate lines for each one, and often quicker, because a free clerk is always called to the next waiting customer. It is also fairer. In the single line, the delay caused by one slow transaction is spread across everyone waiting, instead of landing on whoever happened to choose the wrong lane.

Why, then, do most supermarkets stick with separate lanes? Part of the answer is space: a folded line needs a clear stretch of floor near the front of the store, which is exactly where stores like to put their displays of candy and batteries. Part of it may be that shoppers believe they are good at choosing. Each of us remembers the times we picked the fast lane and forgets the times we did not.

I would gladly give up the small thrill of guessing right for the certainty of being treated like everyone else. The next time I am standing in a long, folded line at the post office, I intend to remind myself that it is moving as fast as any line can, and to leave the magazines alone.

choices: a story of a creamery that failed because its members distrusted each other

item.passage:
Until 1886, the butter of Callow Valley was made in kitchens. Each farm skimmed its own cream, churned it by hand, packed the butter in crocks, and traded it at the store in Brede Ferry for sugar, nails, and cloth. The storekeeper, Lars Halvorsen, sorted the crocks into three grades by smell and color and paid accordingly, though even the best of it brought little in the city, because no two farms' butter tasted alike.

In the spring of 1886 forty-one farmers formed the Callow Valley Cooperative Creamery. They pooled their money to build a frame creamery beside Mill Brook and buy a cream separator, a machine that spun whole milk and threw off the cream far more completely than skimming by hand. Each member hauled his milk to the creamery in the morning, it was weighed at the door, and at the end of each month he was paid by the pound for what he had delivered. Butter from the creamery was uniform, and city buyers paid more for it than the store had ever paid for crock butter.

Payment by weight had one weakness, and within a year everyone knew what it was. A pound of milk from one herd might hold half again as much cream as a pound from another. A farmer whose cows gave thin milk was paid the same as one whose cows gave rich milk, and a farmer who added a bucket of well water to his cans was paid for the water. The creamery's buttermaker, a young man named Otto Brandvold, complained that some mornings the milk ran "blue at the edges."

Brandvold suspected particular members but could prove nothing. Weighing showed only how much milk came in, and the separator mixed every farm's milk together before anyone could see whose was thin.

The answer came from an agricultural college in 1890, in the form of a simple test. A small measured sample of milk was mixed with acid in a narrow glass bottle and spun, and the fat rose into the bottle's marked neck, where it could be read off as a percentage. The creamery bought the equipment the next winter. From March of 1891, each member's milk was sampled at the door and paid for by the pounds of butterfat it contained, rather than by the pounds of milk.

The first payments under the new system were read aloud at the April meeting. Several members found their checks smaller, and two resigned. Most found them larger. Brandvold recorded in his daybook that the milk no longer ran blue, and that the creamery's butter had won second prize at the state fair that September, the first year it had been entered.

Each farm skimmed its own cream, churned it by hand, packed the butter in crocks, and traded it at the store in Brede Ferry for sugar, nails, and cloth. The storekeeper, Lars Halvorsen, sorted the crocks into three grades by smell and color and paid accordingly, though even the best of it brought little in the city, because no two farms' butter tasted alike.

In the spring of 1886 forty-one farmers formed the Callow Valley Cooperative Creamery. They pooled their money to build a frame creamery beside Mill Brook and buy a cream separator, a machine that spun whole milk and threw off the cream far more completely than skimming by hand. Each member hauled his milk to the creamery in the morning, it was weighed at the door, and at the end of each month he was paid by the pound for what he had delivered. Butter from the creamery was uniform, and city buyers paid more for it than the store had ever paid for crock butter.

Payment by weight had one weakness, and within a year everyone knew what it was. A pound of milk from one herd might hold half again as much cream as a pound from another. A farmer whose cows gave thin milk was paid the same as one whose cows gave rich milk, and a farmer who added a bucket of well water to his cans was paid for the water. The creamery's buttermaker, a young man named Otto Brandvold, complained that some mornings the milk ran "blue at the edges."

Brandvold suspected particular members but could prove nothing. Weighing showed only how much milk came in, and the separator mixed every farm's milk together before anyone could see whose was thin.

The answer came from an agricultural college in 1890, in the form of a simple test. A small measured sample of milk was mixed with acid in a narrow glass bottle and spun, and the fat rose into the bottle's marked neck, where it could be read off as a percentage. The creamery bought the equipment the next winter. From March of 1891, each member's milk was sampled at the door and paid for by the pounds of butterfat it contained, rather than by the pounds of milk.

The first payments under the new system were read aloud at the April meeting. Several members found their checks smaller, and two resigned. Most found them larger. Brandvold recorded in his daybook that the milk no longer ran blue, and that the creamery's butter had won second prize at the state fair that September, the first year it had been entered.

item.passage:
Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of every color of the rainbow, from red at one end to violet at the other. On its way to the ground, that light must pass through miles of air, and the air does not treat all of the colors in the same way.

Air is made mostly of nitrogen and oxygen molecules, each far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. When light meets one of these molecules, some of it is scattered: sent off in a new direction. The amount of scattering depends strongly on the color. Blue light, which has a short wavelength, is scattered several times more strongly than red light, which has a long one.

That uneven scattering is why the sky is blue. Look at any patch of sky away from the sun and you are seeing sunlight that has been knocked sideways, perhaps many times, by molecules of air, and because blue light is knocked about far more than red, the scattered light that reaches your eye from every direction is mostly blue.

Violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue and is scattered more strongly still, so it is fair to ask why the sky is not violet. Part of the answer is that sunlight contains less violet than blue to begin with. Part of it lies in our eyes, which are much more sensitive to blue than to violet. The scattered light does contain violet, but we see the mixture as sky blue.

The same process explains a red sunset. When the sun is low, its light reaches us at a slant, passing through far more air than it does at noon. Along that long path, most of the blue is scattered out to the sides, lighting the sky for people elsewhere. What is left to travel straight to your eye is the light that scatters least: the yellows, oranges, and reds.

Clouds follow a different rule. The droplets of water in a cloud are much larger than air molecules, large enough to scatter all colors of light about equally, so a cloud lit by the sun looks white, or gray when it is thick enough to block much of the light. And on the Moon, which has almost no air at all, the daytime sky is black, even with the sun overhead.
